transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Three media organizations have requested an immediate hearing before a federal judge.
CNN, MS Now, and Politico are still blocked from the White House, even though overnight
a federal judge ordered the White House to provide them with immediate access.
President Trump originally blocked them, claiming they "purposely write negative news."
The White House has not given a reason for turning away the journalists this morning.
Meanwhile, President Trump has welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House this
morning for the state visit.
One major focus is likely to be trade.
Daniel Kritenbrink was the U.S. ambassador to Vietnam during the first Trump administration.
He says this summit will likely focus on keeping the trade peace Trump and Xi struck last year.
I think the most important outcome from this summit will be maintaining this so-called
fragile truce between the two powers that was agreed to last year.
If that truce is extended, if that stabilizes the relationship, prevents us from going back
to that trade war, I think that's the single most important outcome.
And actually, I think that's what President Trump is focused on.
He spoke to NPR's morning edition.
Officials in Poland say they suspect Russian sabotage after a fire broke out at a Star
Link satellite communications station. As me Nicholson reports, Warsaw says Moscow is
stepping up its hybrid warfare against NATO countries for supporting Kiev in Russia's
war with Ukraine.
Speaking to public broadcaster TVP, Poland's Deputy Prime Minister Khrushchev Gavkovsky
called the fire an act of sabotage deliberately designed to disable internet access.
The Star Link station in Wieła Krabowska in central Poland serves much of the country
and neighboring Ukraine, including the military. Internet service has been restored.
Gavkovsky says that investigations into the cause of the blaze are underway, but that
it fits the new Russian doctrine of attack.
For NPR News, I'm Esmi Nicholson in Berlin.
Australia's prime minister says an open AI agent hacked into an Australian government
health portal last June. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says he spoke with open AI CEO Sam
Altman. Adam Honkack reports from Sydney.
Anthony Albanese said an open AI agent gained unauthorized access to a portal containing
non-public data from Australia's universal health scheme, Medicare. The tech firm has
confirmed the hack, revealing that it occurred in June when the AI agent was researching
health statistics. They added that the breach was discovered during a review of "misaligned
model activity".
Albanese has called the hack unacceptable and expressed his concerns to open AI boss
Sam Altman. Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles said the impact of the breach was minor.
For NPR News, I'm Adam Hancock.
You're listening to NPR.
Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas delivered a video speech to the UN General
Assembly today the Trump administration would not provide him a visa to come to the US.
Abbas called the move a violation of the US obligation as a host. Meanwhile, Israeli Prime
Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will be at the UN later today to deliver his remarks.
A new analysis of Census Bureau data finds the poverty rate for seniors has risen for
the fifth year in a row. NPR's Jennifer Ludden reports older, lower-income adults are struggling
to save for retirement.
The AARP Foundation analysis found women are far more likely than men to age into poverty.
But its own survey found just under a third of those 50 to 64 reported a significant drop
in household income in the past three months. Foundation President Claire Casey says even
a small disruption, like a car breaking down, can be devastating for low-income workers.
You're much more likely to end up in the long-term unemployed, and you're much more
likely to end up in a job that makes less than the one you were in.
A third of older, low-income adults also said they did not have enough savings to cover
an emergency expense of $100. Jennifer Ludden, NPR News, Washington.
There's a legal fight over late singer Dolly Parton's estate. A Tennessee judge granted
the estate a temporary restraining order against her nephew Brian Seaver and his private security
company. It was Seaver who broke the news of Parton's death. Now, Parton's longtime
manager Danny Nossel is accusing Seaver of trying to get money from the estate. Seaver
denies the allegations he has been fired as head of security. This is NPR.
